detail:
The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) describes bipolar disorder as a condition that usually requires lifelong treatment and does not go away on its own, although symptoms may come and go. Mental health professionals treat bipolar disorder with medications, psychotherapy, or a combination of treatments, and NIMH notes that treatment helps many people, including those with the most severe forms of the disorder, toward better functioning and improved quality of life.

Medication classes clinicians prescribe include mood stabilizers and atypical antipsychotics; NIMH notes that finding the medicines that work best can involve trying several options, and that different medications may be used for an acute mood episode than for long-term management. Bipolar depression is often treated with a mood stabilizer or an atypical antipsychotic, and antidepressants are not used alone because they can trigger a manic episode or rapid cycling; medications that target sleep or anxiety are sometimes added as part of a treatment plan. Psychotherapy approaches clinicians use include cognitive behavioral therapy, family-focused therapy, interpersonal and social rhythm therapy, and psychoeducation, which NIMH describes as providing support, education, and guidance to people with bipolar disorder and their families.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing bipolar disorder.
summary: NIMH describes bipolar disorder treatment as lifelong and clinician-directed, combining medication classes such as mood stabilizers and atypical antipsychotics with psychotherapy approaches including cognitive behavioral and family-focused therapy.
takeaways: bipolar disorder usually requires lifelong treatment
medication classes include mood stabilizers and atypical antipsychotics
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Bipolar disorder: lifelong treatment with medication and psychotherapy
